content: 1. The Single Convention on Narcotic Drugs, established in 1961, serves as the primary international treaty regulating the control of narcotic substances. The International Narcotics Control Board (INCB) oversees its implementation, as detailed in their 2004 publication from Vienna. 2. The INCB's 2008 report, published in 2009, provides an updated analysis of global narcotic control efforts and compliance with the Single Convention. 3. The United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime (UNODC), the World Health Organization (WHO), and the Joint United Nations Programme on HIV/AIDS (UNAIDS) collaborated to create a step-by-step algorithm for procuring controlled substances for drug substitution therapy. This document, accessed in October 2018, is intended to guide national authorities in ensuring the availability of these substances for medical use. 4. The INCB's 2007 guidelines outline the procedures for importing and exporting drugs and precursor reference standards. These guidelines are designed for use by national drug testing laboratories and competent authorities to ensure compliance with international regulations. 5. The 67th World Health Assembly, held in Geneva in May 2014, emphasized the importance of strengthening palliative care as an integral component of comprehensive care throughout the life course. The WHO published this resolution to promote access to palliative care globally. 6. Acetylsalicylic acid (aspirin) is available in suppository (50–150 mg) and tablet (100–500 mg) forms. It is used for mild-to-moderate pain, including dysmenorrhea and headache, as well as for pain and inflammation in rheumatic diseases and musculoskeletal disorders. It is also indicated for pyrexia, acute migraine attacks, and as an antiplatelet agent. Contraindications include hypersensitivity to aspirin or other NSAIDs, children under 16 years (due to Reye’s syndrome risk), active or previous peptic ulceration, bleeding disorders, and use in gout. Precautions include asthma, allergic disease, renal or hepatic impairment, pregnancy, breastfeeding, older age, G6PD deficiency, and dehydration. Adverse effects include gastrointestinal discomfort, nausea, ulceration, bleeding, tinnitus, vertigo, hypersensitivity reactions, and rare cases of edema or blood disorders. 7. Codeine phosphate is available in tablet (15 mg, 30 mg, 60 mg), oral solution (25 mg/5 mL), and injection (60 mg/mL) forms. It is a prodrug of morphine, requiring metabolism by CYP2D6 to exert its analgesic effects. Genetic variability in CYP2D6 metabolism leads to unpredictable efficacy and risks, with ultra-rapid metabolizers at higher risk of morphine toxicity, including respiratory depression. Contraindications include respiratory depression, obstructive airway disease, acute asthma, and risk of paralytic ileus. Adverse effects include constipation, nausea, dizziness, dry mouth, and less commonly, dependence or euphoria. 8. Fentanyl is available as a transmucosal lozenge (200–1600 mcg), transdermal patch (12–100 mcg/hr), and injection (50 mcg/mL). It is indicated for moderate-to-severe persistent pain, particularly in opioid-tolerant patients. Contraindications include hypersensitivity to opioids, acute respiratory depression, and use with monoamine oxidase inhibitors. Precautions include impaired respiratory function, bradycardia, hypotension, and hepatic or renal impairment. Adverse effects include nausea, vomiting, constipation, respiratory depression, muscle rigidity, and rare cases of circulatory depression or seizures. 9. Hydromorphone is available in injection (1–10 mg/mL), tablet (2–8 mg), oral liquid (1 mg/mL), and sustained-release capsule (2–24 mg) forms. It is used for moderate-to-severe persistent pain. Contraindications include hypersensitivity to opioids, acute respiratory depression, and use with monoamine oxidase inhibitors. Precautions include impaired respiratory function, bradycardia, hypotension, and abrupt withdrawal after prolonged use. Adverse effects include nausea, vomiting, constipation, sedation, respiratory depression, and rare cases of circulatory depression or seizures. 10. Ibuprofen is available in tablet form (200 mg, 400 mg) and is used for pain and inflammation in rheumatic diseases, musculoskeletal disorders, dysmenorrhea, headache, and acute migraine attacks. Contraindications include hypersensitivity to NSAIDs, active peptic ulceration, and severe renal or hepatic impairment. Adverse effects include gastrointestinal disturbances, hypersensitivity reactions, headache, dizziness, and rare cases of hepatic damage or aseptic meningitis. 11. Methadone is available in injection (10 mg/mL) and tablet (5 mg) forms. It is used for pain management and opioid substitution therapy.
